title: How Elevators Work
summary: How elevators use cables, a motor-driven wheel, and a counterweight (or oil and a piston) to move safely up and down, and why they made skyscrapers possible.
poll: The elevator is one of the most important inventions in cities.

versions.title: Up and Down
versions.text:
You step in a small room. The door shuts. You push a button. Up you go! You are in a lift.

The lift box rides in a tall shaft. The shaft is like a long tube in the house.

Most lifts hang from thick steel cables. The cables go up and over a big wheel at the top. A motor spins the wheel. Then the box goes up or down.

A heavy block hangs on the far end of the cables. When the box goes up, the block goes down. The block helps lift the box. So the motor does not work so hard.

Is it safe? Yes! Long ago, a man made a brake for lifts. If a cable snaps, the brake grabs the rails. The box stops. It does not fall.

Lifts made tall towers work. Who would climb a hundred floors on foot?

In Riyadh, fast lifts take you up a tall tower. You can stand on a bridge at the top!

Lifts made tall towers useful. Who would want to climb a hundred floors on foot?

In Riyadh, fast lifts take people up a tall tower. They can walk on a bridge near the top!

versions.title: How Elevators Work
versions.text:
You step into a small room, and the doors slide shut. You press a button, and moments later you are rising. You are riding in an elevator, one of the most useful machines in any tall building.

The elevator car travels inside a tall shaft, which is like a long tube running up through the building. Metal rails on the sides of the shaft keep the car steady.

Most elevators in tall buildings hang from strong steel cables. The cables pass over a large wheel at the top, which works like a pulley. An electric motor turns the wheel, and the turning wheel pulls the car up or lowers it down.

At the other end of the cables hangs a heavy block called a counterweight. When the car rises, the counterweight sinks. It is about as heavy as the car plus part of a full load, so it helps balance the car. That means the motor needs much less power.

Short buildings often use a different kind of elevator called a hydraulic elevator. Instead of cables, a strong metal rod under the car is pushed up by oil.

Are elevators safe? Yes. In the 1850s, an inventor named Elisha Otis built a safety brake. If a cable breaks, the brake grabs the rails, and the car stops instead of falling.

Elevators made the skyscraper possible. Without them, few people would climb a hundred floors on foot.

In Riyadh, fast elevators carry visitors up the Kingdom Centre, where they can walk on a bridge near the top.

versions.title: How Elevators Work
versions.text:
You step into a small room, and the doors slide shut behind you. You press a button, and moments later you are rising smoothly. You are riding in an elevator, one of the most important machines in any tall building.

The elevator car travels inside a tall shaft, which is like a long tube running up through the building. Metal rails along the sides of the shaft guide the car and keep it steady.

Most elevators in tall buildings hang from several strong steel cables. These cables pass over a large wheel at the top of the shaft, which works like a pulley. An electric motor turns the wheel, and the turning wheel either pulls the car upward or lowers it gently.

At the other end of the cables hangs a heavy block called a counterweight. When the car rises, the counterweight sinks, and when the car sinks, it rises. The counterweight weighs about as much as the car plus part of a full load, so it helps balance the car. As a result, the motor needs much less power.

Shorter buildings often use a different design called a hydraulic elevator. Instead of cables, a strong metal rod beneath the car is pushed upward by oil under pressure.

Are elevators safe? Yes. In the 1850s, an inventor named Elisha Otis built a safety brake. If a cable ever breaks, the brake grabs the rails, and the car stops instead of falling.

Elevators made the modern skyscraper possible. Without them, very few people would want to climb a hundred floors on foot.

In Riyadh, high-speed elevators carry visitors up the Kingdom Centre, where they can walk across a bridge near the top.

Because it weighs about as much as the car plus part of a full load, the counterweight helps balance the car, so the motor needs much less power.

Shorter buildings often use a different design called a hydraulic elevator. Instead of cables, a strong metal rod beneath the car is pushed upward by oil under pressure.

Are elevators safe? Yes. In the 1850s, an inventor named Elisha Otis developed a safety brake. If a cable ever breaks, the brake clamps onto the rails, and the car stops instead of falling.

versions.title: How Elevators Work
versions.text:
You step into a small room, the doors slide shut behind you, and when you press a button, you begin rising smoothly. You are riding in an elevator, one of the most essential machines in any tall building, although most passengers never think about how it operates.

The elevator car travels inside a vertical shaft, which resembles a long tube running through the building. Metal rails along the sides of the shaft guide the car and keep it steady as it moves.

Most elevators in tall buildings hang from several strong steel cables. These cables pass over a large grooved wheel at the top of the shaft, which functions like a pulley. An electric motor rotates the wheel, and the rotating wheel either pulls the car upward or lowers it gently.

At the opposite end of the cables hangs a heavy block called a counterweight. When the car ascends, the counterweight descends, and when the car descends, the counterweight ascends. Because it weighs about as much as the car plus part of a full load, the counterweight helps balance the car, so the motor requires considerably less power.

Shorter buildings frequently use a different design called a hydraulic elevator. Instead of relying on cables, it uses a strong metal rod beneath the car, which is pushed upward by oil under pressure.

Are elevators safe? Absolutely, because in the 1850s an inventor named Elisha Otis developed a safety brake. If a cable ever breaks, the brake clamps onto the rails, and the car stops instead of plunging downward.

Elevators made the modern skyscraper practical, since without them very few people would be willing to climb a hundred floors on foot every day.

In Riyadh, high-speed elevators carry visitors up the Kingdom Centre, where they can walk across a bridge near the top of the tower.

versions.title: How Elevators Work: The Machine That Built Skylines
versions.text:
You step into a small room, the doors slide shut, and when you press a button, you begin rising smoothly toward the upper floors. Although most passengers never think about it, the elevator is one of the most essential machines in any tall building, and its design combines several clever ideas.

The elevator car travels inside a vertical shaft, guided by metal rails that keep it steady. In most tall buildings, the car hangs from several steel cables that pass over a large grooved wheel, called a sheave, at the top of the shaft. When an electric motor rotates the sheave, friction between the cables and the grooves grips the cables firmly, and this grip, known as traction, allows the turning wheel to raise or lower the car.

At the opposite end of the cables hangs a heavy counterweight. It weighs about as much as the empty car plus part of a full load, so it balances the car, and the motor needs considerably less energy to move it.

Shorter buildings often use hydraulic elevators instead. In this design, oil is pumped under pressure into a cylinder, pushing a piston that lifts the car from below.

Safety is built into every system, and in the 1850s the inventor Elisha Otis developed a mechanism that clamps onto the rails if a cable breaks, stopping the car instead of letting it fall. Modern elevators also hang from several cables, each strong enough to hold the car alone.

Today, computers control most elevators in large buildings, deciding which car should answer each call so that passengers wait as little as possible. In some towers, riders select their floor before entering, and a screen then directs them to the most efficient car. The fastest elevators in the world can climb at more than 70 kilometers per hour, although they speed up gradually so that passengers remain comfortable.

Elevators made the modern skyscraper practical, since few people would climb a hundred floors every day. In Riyadh, high-speed elevators carry visitors up the Kingdom Centre to a bridge near the top of the tower.

Shorter buildings frequently use hydraulic elevators instead. In this design, oil is pumped under pressure into a cylinder, pushing a piston that lifts the car from below, much like a powerful jack.

Safety is built into every system, and in the 1850s the inventor Elisha Otis developed a mechanism that clamps onto the guide rails whenever a cable breaks, stopping the car instead of allowing it to plunge. versions.title: How Elevators Work: The Machine That Built Skylines
versions.text:
You step into a compact room, the doors slide shut, and when you press a button, you begin ascending smoothly toward the upper floors. Although most passengers never consider it, the elevator is one of the most essential machines in any tall building, and its design combines several ingenious principles drawn from physics and mechanical engineering.

The elevator car travels inside a vertical shaft, guided by metal rails that keep it stable. In most tall buildings, the car is suspended from several steel cables that pass over a large grooved wheel, called a sheave, positioned at the top of the shaft. When an electric motor rotates the sheave, friction between the cables and the grooves grips the cables firmly, and this grip, known as traction, enables the rotating wheel to raise or lower the car.

At the opposite end of the cables hangs a substantial counterweight. Because it weighs approximately as much as the empty car plus a portion of a full load, it balances the car, so the motor requires considerably less energy to move it.

Shorter buildings frequently rely on hydraulic elevators instead, in which oil is pumped under pressure into a cylinder, forcing a piston upward so that it lifts the car from below, much like a powerful automobile jack.

Safety is incorporated into every system, and during the 1850s the inventor Elisha Otis developed a mechanism that clamps onto the guide rails whenever a cable breaks, halting the car instead of allowing it to plunge. Modern elevators are also suspended from multiple cables, each sufficiently strong to support the car independently.

Today, sophisticated computers control most elevators in large buildings, calculating which car should answer each call so that passengers wait as briefly as possible. In some towers, riders select their destination before entering, whereupon a screen directs them to the most efficient car. The fastest elevators in the world can ascend at more than 70 kilometers per hour, although they accelerate gradually so that passengers remain comfortable and their ears can adjust to the changing air pressure.

Elevators made the modern skyscraper practical, since few people would willingly climb a hundred floors every day. In Riyadh, high-speed elevators transport visitors up the Kingdom Centre to a bridge near the summit of the tower.

versions.title: How Elevators Work: The Machine That Built Skylines
versions.text:
You step into a compact room, the doors slide shut, and when you press a button, you begin ascending smoothly toward the upper floors. Although most passengers never consider it, the elevator is one of the most essential machines in any tall building, and its design combines several ingenious principles drawn from physics and mechanical engineering that have been refined for more than a century.

The elevator car travels inside a vertical shaft, guided by metal rails that keep it stable. In most tall buildings, the car is suspended from several steel cables that pass over a large grooved wheel, called a sheave, positioned at the top of the shaft. When an electric motor rotates the sheave, friction between the cables and the grooves grips the cables firmly, and this grip, known as traction, enables the rotating wheel to raise or lower the car with remarkable precision.

At the opposite end of the cables hangs a substantial counterweight. Because it weighs approximately as much as the empty car plus a portion of a full load, it balances the car, so the motor requires considerably less energy to move it, which reduces both electricity costs and wear on the equipment.

Shorter buildings frequently rely on hydraulic elevators instead, in which oil is pumped under pressure into a cylinder, forcing a piston upward so that it lifts the car from below, operating much like a powerful automobile jack.

Safety is incorporated into every system, and during the 1850s the inventor Elisha Otis developed a mechanism that clamps onto the guide rails whenever a cable breaks, halting the car instead of allowing it to plunge, and he famously demonstrated it by having the rope above him cut. Modern elevators are also suspended from multiple cables, each sufficiently strong to support the car independently.

Today, sophisticated computers control most elevators in large buildings, continuously calculating which car should answer each call so that passengers wait as briefly as possible. In some towers, riders select their destination before entering, whereupon a screen directs them to the most efficient car. The fastest elevators in the world can ascend at more than 70 kilometers per hour, although they accelerate gradually so that passengers remain comfortable and their ears can adjust to the changing air pressure.

Elevators made the modern skyscraper practical, since few people would willingly climb a hundred floors every day. In Riyadh, high-speed elevators transport visitors up the Kingdom Centre to a bridge near the summit of the tower.
